history.heading: Birthplace of the Buddha
paragraphs: Nepal lies in the Himalayas between China and India. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born at Lumbini in southern Nepal around the 6th or 5th century BCE; it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and pilgrimage centre.
The Kathmandu Valley was ruled by the Licchavi and later the Malla dynasties, under whom the Newar people built the magnificent palaces and temples of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur.

history.heading: Unification and the Ranas
paragraphs: In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah, king of Gorkha, conquered the Kathmandu Valley and unified Nepal. Expansion led to war with the British East India Company in 1814–16; Nepal lost territory but remained independent. Gurkha soldiers have served in the British Army ever since.
From 1846 to 1951 the hereditary Rana prime ministers held real power, keeping Nepal isolated.

history.heading: Monarchy, civil war and republic
paragraphs: In 1951 the monarchy regained power. Multiparty democracy was introduced in 1990. A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 killed around 17,000 people. In 2001 Crown Prince Dipendra killed King Birendra and much of the royal family. King Gyanendra seized absolute power in 2005, but mass protests forced him to step down in 2006.

Nepal became a federal republic in 2008, abolishing the 240-year-old monarchy, and adopted a new constitution in 2015. A devastating earthquake in 2015 killed about 9,000 people. In September 2025 youth-led "Gen Z" protests against corruption and a social media ban turned deadly and forced the prime minister to resign; an interim government led by former chief justice Sushila Karki was formed and scheduled new elections for March 2026.

culture.heading: Peoples and faiths
paragraphs: Nepal has over 120 ethnic groups and over 100 languages; Nepali is the official language. About 80 percent of people are Hindu, and Buddhism is also widespread, with many shared practices. The Kumari, a girl worshipped as a living goddess, is a unique tradition in Kathmandu.

Dashain and Tihar are the biggest festivals. Dal bhat (lentils and rice) is the staple meal, and momos (dumplings) are popular. Sherpa people are famous for their mountaineering skills; Mount Everest (Sagarmatha), the world's highest peak, lies on the border with China.

politics.heading: Federal parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Nepal is a federal parliamentary republic with seven provinces. The prime minister leads the government, and the president is head of state. Politics since 2008 has been unstable, with frequent changes of government among the Nepali Congress, the Communist Party (UML) and the Maoist party, fuelling public frustration with corruption.

economy.heading: Remittances and tourism
paragraphs: Nepal is one of the poorer countries in Asia. Remittances from millions of Nepalis working in the Gulf, Malaysia and India make up around a quarter of GDP. Agriculture employs most people. Tourism, including trekking and mountaineering, is important, and Nepal has large hydropower potential and exports electricity to India.
The Nepalese rupee is pegged to the Indian rupee, and India is the main trading partner.
